In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
WS1 and WS2 are genetically heterogeneous disorders and that the molecular cause is not found in approximately one third of the cases.
the molecular diagnosis of WS, performed in a large sample of Brazilian patients, allowed us to find a causative mutation in approximately 38.8% of the cases.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
38.8% of the cases had a causative molecular diagnosis, 12.2%, a copy-number-variant (CNV), and 49.0%, no molecular diagnosis.

the molecular diagnosis of WS, in this sample of Brazilian patients, revealed a total of 38.8% of causative variants, 12.2%, 31.6%, and 7.1% of them being large deletions, SNV, and indels, respectively.
WS1 is more frequently caused by large copy-number-variations in the PAX3 gene, while WS2 seems to be more often due to small mutations in SOX10.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the molecular diagnosis of WS, in a Brazilian sample, is feasible in about 40% of patients, and that MLPA is a valuable tool for the detection of causative copy-number-variants.
the molecular screening of the six known WS genes is essential for a complete molecular characterization of the syndrome.
the molecular screening in WS should include both SNV and CNV detection, as both are equally frequent and, together, are able to explain most of the causative mutations.
